articles.title: ARIA in patients treated with lecanemab (BAN2401) in a phase 2 study in early Alzheimer's disease.
articles.snippet: Honig LS, Barakos J, Dhadda S, Kanekiyo M, Reyderman L, Irizarry M et al. | Alzheimer's & dementia (New York, N. Y.) | 2023 | Journal Article
articles.full_summary: This phase 2 study of lecanemab in early Alzheimer's disease reports a low incidence of ARIA-E, which was generally asymptomatic and mild-to-moderate, occurring early in treatment and more frequently in ApoE4 homozygous carriers.
articles.key_finding: In the phase 2 core and OLE, there was a low incidence of ARIA-E (<10%), with <3% symptomatic cases.
articles.population: patients with early Alzheimer's disease

articles.title: Updated safety results from phase 3 lecanemab study in early Alzheimer's disease.
articles.snippet: Honig LS, Sabbagh MN, van Dyck CH, Sperling RA, Hersch S, Matta A et al. | Alzheimer's research & therapy | 2024-May-10 | Journal Article; Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial
articles.full_summary: This phase 3 study of lecanemab in early Alzheimer's disease reports on the safety profile, including the incidence of ARIA-H and ARIA-E, and their association with ApoE ε4 carriers.
articles.key_finding: In the Core + OLE, the most common adverse events in the lecanemab group (> 10%) were infusion-related reactions (24.5%), ARIA with hemosiderin deposits (ARIA-H) microhemorrhages (16.0%), COVID-19 (14.7%), ARIA with edema (ARIA-E; 13.6%), and headache (10.3%).
articles.population: participants with early Alzheimer's disease

articles.full_summary: The FDA drug label for LEQEMBI (lecanemab) details its indications, dosage, warnings regarding ARIA, and mechanism of action for Alzheimer's disease.

articles.population: patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia stage of Alzheimer's disease

articles.title: Lecanemab for treatment of individuals with early Alzheimer's Disease (AD) who are apolipoprotein E ε4 (ApoE ε4) non-carriers or heterozygotes.

articles.title: Lecanemab over a two-year duration: Key insights from a regional specialty medical center.

articles.full_summary: This observational study from a regional medical center evaluates the incidence of ARIA and other adverse events associated with lecanemab in patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease.
articles.key_finding: Of the 175 patients who underwent at least one surveillance brain MRI following lecanemab initiation, 39 (22.3 %) had evidence of ARIA (both ARIA-H and ARIA-E: 13 [33.3 %]; solitary ARIA-H: 17 [43.6 %]; and solitary ARIA-E: 9 [23.1 %]).
articles.population: patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease

articles.title: Safety and efficacy of lecanemab for Alzheimer's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
articles.snippet: Qiao Y, Chi Y, Zhang Q, Ma Y | Frontiers in aging neuroscience | 2023 | Systematic Review; Journal Article
articles.full_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of four randomized controlled trials found that lecanemab was beneficial in stabilizing or slowing the decrease in cognitive and functional scores in early AD patients. It also reported increased risks for ARIA-E and ARIA-H.
articles.key_finding: It is reported that lecanemab was beneficial to stabilize or slow down the decrease in CDR-SB (WMD: -0.45; 95% CI: -0.64, -0.25; p < 0.00001), ADCOMS (WMD: -0.05; 95% CI: -0.07, -0.03; p < 0.00001), ADAS-cog (WMD: -1.11; 95% CI: -1.64, -0.57; p < 0.0001), amyloid PET SUVr (WMD: -0.15; 95% CI: -0.48, 0.19; p = 0.38), amyloid burden on PET (WMD:-35.44; 95% CI: -65.22,-5.67; p = 0.02), adverse events
articles.population: AD patients with MCI or AD

articles.title: Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer's Disease.

articles.full_summary: This phase 3 trial investigates the efficacy and safety of lecanemab in early Alzheimer's disease, showing reduced amyloid markers and less cognitive decline compared to placebo, but with associated adverse events including ARIA-E.
articles.key_finding: Lecanemab reduced markers of amyloid in early Alzheimer's disease and resulted in moderately less decline on measures of cognition and function than placebo at 18 months but was associated with adverse events.
articles.population: persons with early Alzheimer's disease (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease)

articles.title: APOE-guided lecanemab dosing dissociates ARIA-E from ARIA-H: The K-ROAD study.
articles.snippet: Kang H, Jang H, Ahn J, Na DL, Lee JH, Kim EJ et al. | Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association | 2026-Aug | Journal Article; Multicenter Study
articles.full_summary: This multicenter study investigated APOE genotype-guided lecanemab escalation and its effect on ARIA-E and ARIA-H incidence in early Alzheimer's disease patients.
articles.key_finding: ARIA-E incidence was 2.0% in non-carriers and 6.2% in εε4/εε4 homozygotes (εε4/εε4-versus-non-carrier OR 3.25, versus 8.49 in Clarity AD and 8.32 in Japan post-marketing surveillance). Any ARIA-H was independently predicted by baseline cerebral microbleeds, white matter hyperintensity (WMH), age, and APOE εε4 allele dose (aORs 1.23, 1.50, 1.04, 1.75).
articles.population: patients with early Alzheimer's disease

Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) represent the most clinically important safety concern, yet
articles.full_summary: This narrative review synthesizes evidence on fluid and imaging biomarkers for ARIA risk stratification and treatment-response monitoring in lecanemab therapy for early Alzheimer's disease.
articles.key_finding: APOE ε4 genotype and baseline MRI markers of cerebral amyloid angiopathy are the only established, clinically actionable ARIA risk stratifiers.

articles.title: Lecanemab Treatment in a Specialty Memory Clinic.
articles.snippet: Paczynski M, Hofmann A, Posey Z, Gregersen M, Rudman M, Ellington D et al. | JAMA neurology | 2025-Jul-01 | Journal Article
articles.full_summary: A real-world study in a specialty memory clinic found lecanemab treatment for early AD to be feasible with manageable adverse events, including ARIA.

response.global_summary:
Lecanemab, a monoclonal antibody targeting aggregated forms of beta-amyloid, has demonstrated efficacy in slowing cognitive decline in patients with early Alzheimer's disease (AD) [2][5][6][11]. Multiple randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews indicate that lecanemab significantly reduces clinical decline on measures such as the Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB), Alzheimer's Disease Composite Score (ADCOMS), and Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-cog) over 18 months compared to placebo [5][6][11]. For instance, a meta-analysis reported a **weighted mean difference of -0.45** for CDR-SB, **-0.05** for ADCOMS, and **-1.11** for ADAS-cog, all statistically significant [5]. Another randomized controlled trial (RCT) specifically noted a reduction in clinical decline on CDR-SB at 18 months in the *ApoEε4 heterozygotes or non-carriers subgroup* [3]. An analysis in the Asian region from the Clarity AD trial also showed a **24% slowing of decline** in CDR-SB at 18 months [16]. Beyond clinical outcomes, lecanemab has been shown to substantially reduce amyloid plaque load and amyloid burden on PET scans [5][15].

However, treatment with lecanemab is associated with amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), which include ARIA with edema (ARIA-E) and ARIA with hemosiderin deposition (ARIA-H) [2][17]. The incidence of ARIA varies across studies, but it is a common adverse event. In a phase 3 study, ARIA-E occurred in **13.6%** of patients and ARIA-H in **16.0%** [1]. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that the relative risk of ARIA in patients treated with lecanemab was **4.35 times higher** than in control groups, with significantly higher risks for both ARIA-E and ARIA-H [11]. Real-world cohort studies have reported ARIA incidence rates ranging from **7.1%** (mostly asymptomatic and mild) in one cohort [13] to **18.6%** (mostly asymptomatic) in another [9], and **22.3%** in a regional specialty medical center, where **33.3%** of those had both ARIA-H and ARIA-E [4]. Another real-world study observed ARIA in **22%** of patients over an average of **6.5 months** of treatment, with **15%** developing ARIA-E with or without ARIA-H and **6.7%** developing isolated ARIA-H [19]. A phase 2 study reported a low incidence of ARIA-E (**<10%**), with **<3%** symptomatic cases [0]. Overall, approximately **21%** of participants in clinical trials developed ARIA [12].

The risk of ARIA is significantly influenced by the apolipoprotein E ε4 (ApoE ε4) genotype [7][8][12][14]. Patients who are homozygous for ApoEε4 have a higher incidence of ARIA [12][14]. For example, one cohort study found ARIA-E incidence was **2.0%** in non-carriers and **6.2%** in ε4/ε4 homozygotes, with the odds ratio for ε4/ε4 versus non-carrier being **3.25** [7]. Baseline cerebral microbleeds, white matter hyperintensity (WMH), and age are also independent predictors of ARIA-H [7]. While most ARIA events are asymptomatic, symptomatic cases can occur and may require hospitalization and treatment discontinuation [0][9]. Infusion-related reactions are also common, reported in **24.5%** of the lecanemab group in one phase 3 study [1] and **26.4%** in a systematic review [15]. Long-term data from an open-label extension study suggest that ARIA rates were low after **6 months** and not associated with long-term progression [18].

key_findings.text: Lecanemab significantly slows cognitive and functional decline in patients with early Alzheimer's disease.
Lecanemab substantially reduces amyloid plaque load and amyloid burden in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's disease.
Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), including ARIA-E (edema) and ARIA-H (hemosiderin deposition), are common adverse events associated with lecanemab treatment.
The incidence of ARIA-E and ARIA-H varies, with reported rates for any ARIA ranging from 7.1% to 22.3% in real-world settings and up to 21% in clinical trials.
The ApoE ε4 genotype, particularly homozygosity, is a significant risk factor for developing ARIA, especially ARIA-E.
Baseline cerebral microbleeds, white matter hyperintensity, and age are independent predictors of ARIA-H.
Infusion-related reactions are a common adverse event with lecanemab, occurring in approximately 24.5% to 26.4% of patients.
Most ARIA events are asymptomatic, but symptomatic cases can occur and may necessitate hospitalization and treatment discontinuation.
Long-term data suggest that ARIA rates are low after 6 months of treatment and are not associated with long-term disease progression.

evidence_gaps: The sources do not provide detailed information on the long-term clinical outcomes beyond 18 months for lecanemab treatment.
The sources do not extensively cover the management strategies for symptomatic ARIA events or the long-term consequences of ARIA on patient health.
The sources do not provide a comprehensive comparison of lecanemab's efficacy and safety profile against other anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies, beyond a mention in one meta-analysis [11].
